bk.btn.group.d: A small gap apart, the main action first; on a narrow screen they wrap onto the next line.
bk.btn.hover.d: The label is underlined. The colours stay the same, so nothing flashes.
bk.btn.label: Label
bk.btn.label.d: Atkinson Hyperlegible Bold, 16 pixels, in sentence case. A verb first: "Choose files", "Download the beta".
bk.btn.lede: A button says what it does, in one or two words. On this website the buttons are drawn as below; in the apps they are the platform's own (Material 3 on Android, the desktop's buttons on Linux), with the same rules. On Android, icon buttons follow Material 3 Expressive and turn into a rounded square while pressed.
bk.btn.main.d: Filled with the accent colour, label in the on-accent colour. One per view, for what most people do next.
bk.btn.no1: Never two filled buttons in one view.
bk.btn.no2: No button with only an icon and no word.
bk.btn.no3: No capitals, exclamation marks or vague labels such as "OK" or "Click here".
bk.btn.no4: A link that takes you somewhere looks like a link; a button does something.
bk.btn.other.d: A 1 pixel border in the outline colour, label in ink, no fill. Use as many as the view needs.
bk.btn.shape.d: On this website, fully rounded ends. No shadow, gradient or glow.
bk.btn.size.d: 56 pixels tall, 24 pixels of space at each side; as wide as the label, or the full width of a phone screen for the main action in the apps.
bk.btn.text.d: Bold text in the accent colour, no frame, right next to what it acts on, such as copying a command.
bk.cmp.card.d: 28 pixel corners, a hairline instead of a shadow. A card frames only something to tap or something important to check, such as a code. Codes stay in English and read left to right in every language.
bk.cmp.focus.d: A 3 pixel ring in the accent colour, 3 pixels away, on everything that can be reached with the keyboard. Touch targets are at least 44 pixels.
bk.cmp.lang.d: A plain pill with a small arrow. Every language is listed under its own name, never as a flag.
bk.cmp.state.d: A word with a dot: filled when available, hollow when still on the way. The state is in the word and the shape, not only in the colour.
bk.cmp.title: Buttons and components
bk.col.accent: The one main action, links, the focus ring. Once per view.
bk.col.c1.d: Ink on paper 14.4:1, paper on night 16.6:1.
bk.col.c2.d: Violet on paper 5.1:1, glow on night 6.8:1. On the raised surface the accent and success colours are only for large text and icons.
bk.col.error: Something went wrong. Always with an icon or a word.
bk.col.glow: The mark and the accent on dark grounds.
bk.col.lede: The apps use the colours of the system they run on: Material You on Android, the desktop theme on Linux. The Aurora palette below is used when the system gives no colours, and on this website. Text on the page ground passes 4.5:1 in both themes.
bk.col.mist: Quiet raised surface on light grounds.
bk.col.onaccent: Text on an accent fill; dark in the dark theme, because the accent is lighter there.
bk.col.outline: Borders of fields and outlined buttons.
bk.col.paper: Light ground; the mark on the app icon.
bk.col.raised: Quiet second surface, such as the Receive card.
bk.col.success: Finished. Always with an icon or a word, never colour alone.
bk.col.title: Colour
bk.col.tokens: Colour roles, light and dark theme
bk.col.violet: The mark and the accent on light grounds.
bk.done.d: When the files have arrived, the mark rests with a check in its circle: paper white on the light theme, ink on the dark.
bk.f.fonts.d: Bricolage Grotesque and Atkinson Hyperlegible are free under the SIL Open Font License; get them from their makers or from Google Fonts.
bk.f.mono.d: Only where colour cannot be printed, such as stamps or engraving.
bk.files.lede: Vector files (SVG) for print and screens, and PNG files with a transparent background. Use them as they are.
bk.files.title: Downloads
bk.ic.r1: In the apps, icons come from the system: Material icons on Android, the desktop's icon theme on Linux (Breeze on Plasma, symbolic icons elsewhere).
bk.ic.r2: Icons take the colour of the text next to them; only status icons use the success or error colour.
bk.ic.r3: An icon is never the only label: a word goes with it.
bk.ic.r4: Drawings on the website are plain lines on a 24-unit grid, 1.75 units thick, with round ends, like these devices.
bk.ic.r5: Icons that point a way, such as a back arrow, mirror in right-to-left languages; the mark never does.
bk.ic.title: Icons
bk.icon.d: The mark in paper white on violet, half the tile's width. On Android's adaptive icon it is smaller, so its corner stays well clear of every launcher's shape; the one-colour layer is white.
bk.lede: One mark, one accent colour, two typefaces. Everything else comes from the system TotalDrop runs on. This page shows the parts, how to use them and where to download them.
bk.logo.dark.d: The mark turns bright violet and the name paper white.
bk.logo.title: Logo and app icon
bk.logo.word.d: The mark, then the name in Bricolage Grotesque ExtraBold. The name is one word with two capitals and is never translated or transliterated.
bk.mark.build.d: On a 112-unit square: a circle of radius 42 centred at 55, 57, its top right quarter filled out to a square corner at 97, 15. The circle sits one unit left and down of the centre, so the heavier corner side looks centred.
bk.mark.lede: The mark is called Köşe, Turkish for corner: a circle with one square corner. The circle is the whole (Total); the corner turns it into a drop (Drop) and points where the file goes. It is also the corner of a file and of a device's screen.
bk.mark.min.d: 16 pixels wide, as in a browser tab. The same drawing works at every size; there is no separate small version.
bk.mark.rtl: In right-to-left languages the layout mirrors, but the mark does not: at rest its corner is always at the top right.
bk.mark.space.d: Keep at least half the radius (21 units, a quarter of the mark's width) free on every side. Nothing else enters this area: no text, no edge, no other logo.
bk.mark.title: The mark
bk.mo.cycle.d: 3.2 seconds, repeating: four quarters, back where it began.
bk.mo.devices.d: On the home page, a desktop, a phone, a laptop and a tablet sit outside the clear space, one where the corner points after each quarter; the one it reaches lights up. They are not part of the mark and the apps do not show them.
bk.mo.lede: While a transfer runs, the mark turns clockwise a quarter at a time around the centre of its circle, and its corner points at each side in turn: from every device to every device. The website, the Android app and the Linux app use the same values.
bk.mo.only: This is the brand's only animation. Screens move with the platform's own transitions: no bounce, sparkle or confetti.
bk.mo.quarter.d: 0.8 seconds: a 90° turn in 0.6 seconds, then a 0.2 second rest.
bk.mo.reduce.d: When the system asks for less motion, the mark stays at rest and progress is shown by the bar and the percentage.
bk.mo.title: Motion
bk.no.label: Don't
bk.no.lede: The mark is one flat colour, used as it is. These are the common mistakes.
bk.no.logos: Do not put platform or manufacturer logos (Apple, Android, Windows) next to the mark; use plain device drawings instead.
bk.no.title: What not to do
bk.no2: Stretch the circle into an ellipse.
bk.no3: Put it in a frame, ring or box.
bk.no5: Add a gradient, shadow or outline.
bk.no6: Turn it at rest: the corner stays at the top right.
bk.no7: Mirror it, also not for right-to-left languages.
bk.no8: Place it on a busy image or a ground with too little contrast.
bk.p.lede: TotalDrop follows Dieter Rams: every element has a job, and whatever has none is left out.
bk.p.title: Less, but better
bk.p1.d: The apps take their colours, light or dark theme, icons and windows from the system, and on Linux the fonts too. Only the mark and its colours stay the same everywhere.
bk.p2.d: Violet marks the one thing to do next, links and the focus ring. Everything else is ink on paper.
bk.p3.d: No shadows, gradients, glass or glow. Surfaces are told apart by a hairline or a quieter tone; size and position make the hierarchy.
bk.p4.d: Short sentences that say what happens. No exclamation marks, no invented numbers, no promises the code does not keep.
bk.sp.24: Inside a card, screen edge (16 on phones)
bk.sp.8: Icon to label, heading to text
bk.sp.note: Start from these steps. Gaps inside one component, such as between two buttons, may be smaller.
bk.sp.rnote: These are the corners of this website. In the apps, buttons, fields and cards follow the platform; on Linux, the desktop's rounding.
bk.sp.title: Spacing and corners
bk.symbolic.d: In system bars and menus the mark alone, in the colour of the text around it.
bk.title: The TotalDrop brand
bk.type.body: Everything else: running text, buttons and fields. Made by the Braille Institute so that similar letters such as I, l and 1 stay apart.
bk.type.display: Headings, codes, step numbers and the wordmark, in bold and extra bold, never under 18 pixels. Large headings are set tight.
bk.type.lede: Two open typefaces under the SIL Open Font License, served from this site. Where a script is not covered, the system's own font takes over.
bk.type.rules: Lines of running text stay under 44rem. Figures that line up, such as sizes and percentages, use tabular numbers. Letter spacing is removed in Arabic-script languages, where it would break the joins.
bk.type.title: Type
bk.vo.title: Voice
bk.vo1.d: A button names its action: "Choose files", "Accept". An error says what went wrong and what to do next, without apologising.
bk.vo2.d: Only the first word and names start with a capital. No capitals for emphasis, no emoji, no exclamation marks.
bk.vo3.d: "End-to-end encrypted" only where it is. A privacy promise says the same as the privacy policy, and limits are written where people see them.
bk.vo4.d: Every text a person reads is written for all of TotalDrop's languages, with local number formats. Transfer codes and check words stay in English, so both devices show the same words.
bk.use.title: Using the name and mark
bk.use.lede: TotalDrop is open source, but its licences cover the code, not the TotalDrop name and mark. These rules exist so that an app called TotalDrop really comes from this project.
bk.use1.d: Link to totaldrop.app and mention TotalDrop in articles, reviews, videos and lessons, with the name and the unchanged mark. There is no need to ask.
bk.use2.d: Linux distributions, AUR and F-Droid may ship TotalDrop under its name when the code is unchanged. Patches needed only to build or install it are fine.
bk.use3.t: Build something that works with it
bk.use3.d: The protocol is open. Your app or library may say that it works with TotalDrop, as long as its own name does not contain TotalDrop and it does not use the mark.
bk.use4.t: Changed the code? Use your own name
bk.use4.d: The licences let you change the code. Publish your version under its own name and mark. You may say that it is based on TotalDrop, but not suggest that TotalDrop endorses it.
bk.use.no1: Present anything as an official TotalDrop release, partner or endorsed product.
bk.use.no2: Use a name or domain that can be mistaken for TotalDrop.
bk.use.no3: Publish an app called TotalDrop on Google Play, the App Store, the Microsoft Store or the Snap Store.
bk.use.ask: Selling goods with the name or mark, and any other commercial use not covered here, needs written permission: write to hello@totaldrop.app. TotalDrop is not a registered trademark; these rules say how the project looks after its name.
bk.use.accounts: TotalDrop's official accounts on the web and social media are these. An account that uses the name but is not listed here does not belong to the project.
bk.use.rules: Full rules in the repository, in Turkish

dl.verify.title: Check what you install
dl.verify.v1: Get TotalDrop only from Google Play, from this page or from the project's GitHub releases. We do not publish anywhere else.
dl.verify.v2: Every release on GitHub lists SHA-256 checksums. Compare them before you run a file.
dl.verify.v3: Everything is built from the public source code, which you can read and build yourself.
dl.verify.v4: On Linux, install the file you downloaded with sudo pacman -U, sudo apt install ./ or sudo dnf install ./ and its name.

don.audit.d1: TotalDrop promises that nobody in between can read your files. A promise like that should be checked by people who did not write the code. Before version 1.0, an independent firm will review the protocol, the cryptography and the code that handles untrusted input, and the full report will be published.
don.audit.d2: Audits of this kind are priced in tens of thousands of dollars; published quotes for similar work go as high as 64,000 USD. We expect 20,000 to 60,000 USD, depending on the firm and the scope. Version 1.0 waits for it.
don.audit.title: The big one: an independent security audit
don.b1.f: The address of the site and of every server, registered at cost with Cloudflare
don.b2.f: The site, the rendezvous server and the relay. Free until relay traffic passes the free daily limits; then 5 USD a month with 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds included
don.b3.f: Apple lets only signed and notarised apps run without warnings on iPhone, iPad and Mac
don.b4.f: Without a signature Windows warns of an unknown publisher. Certum's certificate for open-source developers: 69 EUR the first year with card and reader, 49 EUR after. Microsoft's own service is not offered to individuals outside the US and Canada
don.b5.f: Tells each device its public address, so two devices can connect directly
don.b6.f: The code, automatic builds and release downloads, free for open source
don.b7.f: Publishing the Android app; a one-time fee, already paid
don.budget.title: Every cost, line by line
don.how.h1: Donations go through GitHub Sponsors, once or every month.
don.how.h2: They pay only for the costs on this page. When a cost is added or changes, this page changes first.
don.how.h3: Every month we publish what came in and where it went, here and in the project's repository.
don.how.h4: A donation buys no features, no priority and no influence over the app. Everyone gets the same TotalDrop.
don.how.title: How the money is handled
don.lede: TotalDrop is free for everyone and stays that way: no ads, no premium tier, no investors, no data to sell. Some things still cost money. This page lists every one of them, so you can see exactly what a donation pays for.

hero.lede: TotalDrop moves files directly from your device to theirs, encrypted end to end. You share a short code; nobody in between can read what you send. No account, no email, no phone number.
hero.title: Send a file straight to another device.
how.note: Across the internet, the two devices connect directly wherever they can. When a router or firewall is in the way, the encrypted transfer goes through our relay, which cannot read it.
how.s1.d: Any type, as many as you like. The receiver gets only what you chose.
how.s2.d: A number and two words, like 7-harbor-rocket. It works once and then expires.
how.s3.d: Both screens show the same four words. If they match, the connection is yours alone.

rm.d1.d: TotalDrop Protocol v0: transfer codes with CPace, Noise XXpsk3 with post-quantum ML-KEM-768, QUIC with single-use keys. Written down so anyone can build a compatible app.
rm.d2.d: Send and receive from a terminal on Linux, macOS and Windows.
rm.d3.d: Send and receive with a code, in your language, following the phone's colours. On Google Play by invitation.
rm.d4.d: Qt 6 and native Wayland. Follows the theme of KDE Plasma, Hyprland and Omarchy live. Packages for Arch, Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora.
rm.d5.d: Both devices listen and dial, so a firewall on one side no longer stops a transfer.
rm.l1.d: Native apps, once donations cover Apple's developer account.
rm.l2.d: Send to someone who is not online: an encrypted copy waits up to 7 days, and only the link opens it.
rm.l3.d: Optional: no email, phone, password or number to type. Your devices hold the account; your own devices send to each other, and saved contacts send to you, without a code.
rm.l3.t: An account the server never keeps
rm.l4.d: Pair once, check four words, and send to that person again without a code.
rm.l5.d: The relay reached over Tor, with padded sizes, so not even our servers see your IP address.
rm.lede: Dates are aims, not promises: a feature ships only when it is safe. Every step can be followed in the open repository.
rm.n1.d: Devices find their public address with STUN and connect directly through most home routers. When that is impossible, the encrypted traffic goes through our relay on Cloudflare, which cannot read it.
rm.n2.d: Relay only: the other side never learns your IP address.
rm.n2.t: Privacy mode in the command line
rm.title: What is coming to TotalDrop
rm.v1.d: An outside firm reviews the protocol, the cryptography and the code that handles untrusted input. The full report is published.
rm.v2.d: A ProVerif or Tamarin proof that the hybrid handshake keeps its promises.
rm.v2.t: A formal model of the handshake
rm.v3.d: Device keys add ML-DSA-65 next to Ed25519, so even a future quantum computer cannot impersonate you.
rm.v4.d: People who opt in can use relays run by others, from a signed list.
rm.x1.d: Point the phone at the sender's screen instead of typing the code.
rm.x1.t: Scan the QR code with the camera
rm.x2.d: Open a link, type the code, save the files. Nothing to install, still end-to-end encrypted.
rm.x3.d: A dropped connection picks up where it stopped, without sending what already arrived.
rm.x4.d: A transfer that started through the relay moves to a direct path as soon as one opens.
rm.x5.d: A native Windows 11 app. Signed once donations cover the certificate.
rm.x6.d: Install and update with your AUR helper.
rm.x7.d: One switch in Settings: everything goes through the relay, so the other device never learns your IP address.
rm.x8.d: .deb and .rpm packages for ARM64 computers such as Snapdragon X and NVIDIA RTX Spark.
rm.x9.d: The apps and this site in 35 languages, with your region's number formats. Native speakers are checking the drafts.

sec.f1.d: Files are encrypted on your device and decrypted only on the receiver's. The keys never exist anywhere else.
sec.f2.d: The code turns into a key through a PAKE handshake, so a wrong guess fails at once and the attempt is burned. Key exchange includes post-quantum ML-KEM.
sec.f2.t: The code cannot be guessed offline
sec.f3.d: It sees your IP address and the code's number, never the words, the file names or the files. It keeps no logs.
sec.f4.d: Every line is public. Version 1.0 ships only after an independent security audit.
sec.title: Only you and the receiver can open it
why.cmp.caption: How TotalDrop compares with the usual ways to send a file
why.cmp.q1: No copy stored on a company's server
why.r1.d: Files go from your device to theirs. No copy waits on a company's server, and no link expires in a week.
why.r2.d: No email, no phone number, no sign-up. A short code is all two devices need.
why.r3.d: Android, Linux and the command line today; Windows, macOS and iOS on the way. Phone to laptop, any brand to any brand.
why.r4.d: Whole folders, long videos, original-quality photos. Only your disk and your connection set the limit.
why.r5.d: Four words on both screens prove nobody is in the middle. Encryption is end to end and post-quantum.
why.r6.d: Open source under the GPL, paid for by donations. No ads, no tracking, no premium tier.
why.title: Why TotalDrop
